doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Television versus film work and the clique of composers
summary: TV assignments were easier; a few composers dominate film.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Was it easier writing music for television than it was writing music for films? I notice on the film credits [that] these are primarily films that were aimed toward a black market in the black community, films like Cleopatra Jones. I’m just wondering if it was any easier to get work as far as television writing than it was writing for feature films.

Yes, it was easier. Al Bart had an easier time of getting assignments for me for television than for feature films. If the truth be told, there are only a few feature film composers who do most of the films in Hollywood. It's a very self-contained little clique of composers. It's Goldsmith and Schifrin and Pat . . .

I’d say you could name between fifteen or twenty – and that's it – who do most of the films. That was the way it was then. I don’t know how it is now. I have been out of that situation for a number of years. And far be it for me to characterize what the attitude and the climate or the environment is now as far as the selection of composers for a given film project by a film production company. I really can’t say.
If you look at the credits on the film, it’s the same.
Yes, 'cause I see the same names. The only one who has emerged that's probably bigger than life is Williams.
He's much bigger than life. Yeah. Right.
